energyBalance.warming: Warming: more energy in than out
energyBalance.cooling: Cooling: more energy out than in
energyBalance.distanceAxis: Distance from the star (AU, log scale)
energyBalance.explanation1: A planet absorbs starlight on the disc it shows the star, and radiates infrared from its whole surface. Its temperature rises or falls until the infrared going out equals the starlight coming in: that is its equilibrium temperature.
energyBalance.explanation2: The disc has a quarter of the area of the sphere, so a planet that spreads the heat around (it spins, or winds carry the heat) divides the absorbed starlight by 4. A planet that keeps one face to its star and moves no heat divides it by only 2, so its day side is hotter.
energyBalance.explanation3: Albedo is the fraction of starlight a planet reflects: fresh snow and bright clouds reflect a lot, dark rock very little.
energyBalance.explanation4: Compare the equilibrium temperature with the measured surface temperature. For airless Mercury and thin-aired Mars they agree; Earth is 33 K warmer and Venus about 500 K warmer. The Greenhouse screen explains the difference.

greenhouse.verdictVapour: Water would boil away as vapour.
greenhouse.verdictSupercritical: Too hot and dense: water is a supercritical fluid.
greenhouse.explanation1: Most sunlight passes through an atmosphere to the ground, but gases such as water vapour and CO₂ absorb the infrared the ground gives off. They re-emit part of it back down, so the surface must warm until enough infrared escapes from the cold upper layers to balance the sunlight.
greenhouse.explanation2: The greenhouse strength τ (infrared optical depth) measures how opaque the atmosphere is to infrared. With τ ≈ 0.85 this model gives Earth its 288 K; Venus needs τ ≈ 140.
greenhouse.explanation3: Warm is not enough for liquid water: the air must also press hard enough. Below the triple point (611 Pa, about 0.006 bar) water goes straight from ice to vapour. Mars sits right at that pressure.
greenhouse.explanation4: This is a teaching model: real greenhouse warming depends on which gases absorb at which wavelengths, on clouds, and on convection.

zoneEdges.planetMass: Planet mass for the inner edge
zoneEdges.noPlanets: Choose a real star to see its planets.
zoneEdges.outsideFit: Below 2600 K the fits stop: edges drawn for 2600 K.
zoneEdges.explanationTitle: The edges of the habitable zone
zoneEdges.explanation1: The habitable zone is the range of distances where a rocky planet with water and a CO₂ atmosphere could keep liquid water on its surface. Its edges come from climate models (Kopparapu et al. 2013, 2014).
zoneEdges.explanation2: Inner edge — runaway greenhouse: with too much starlight, warm oceans put so much water vapour in the air that the planet cannot radiate the extra heat. The oceans boil away. Outer edge — maximum greenhouse: far out, adding CO₂ eventually reflects more starlight than it traps, so no atmosphere keeps the surface above freezing.
zoneEdges.explanation3: The optimistic edges come from history: Venus may have kept water until about a billion years ago, and Mars had liquid water 3.8 billion years ago.
zoneEdges.explanation4: The zone tilts on the diagram because a cooler star gives more of its light in the infrared, which water and CO₂ absorb well: a planet around a red dwarf warms with less total starlight. A heavier planet can sit a little closer in.

agingStar.redDwarf: Red dwarf (0.3 M<sub>☉</sub>), planet at 0.16 AU
agingStar.aStar: A star (2 M<sub>☉</sub>), planet at 5 AU
agingStar.zoomLate: Zoom in on the late stages
agingStar.timeInZonePattern: Time in the conservative zone so far: {{value}}
agingStar.locked: An Earth-like planet here is tidally locked.
agingStar.engulfed: The star has swallowed the planet.
agingStar.explanation1: Stars brighten as they age on the main sequence, so the habitable zone moves outward. The Sun was about 26 % dimmer 4.6 billion years ago, yet Earth had liquid water: the faint young Sun puzzle, solved by a stronger early greenhouse.
agingStar.explanation2: The continuously habitable zone (hatched) holds the distances that stayed habitable for the whole of the chosen time. A planet needs a long stay for life to develop.
agingStar.explanation3: Light stars live much longer than heavy ones: a 0.3 M<sub>☉</sub> red dwarf stays on the main sequence for about 400 billion years, a 2 M<sub>☉</sub> star for about one billion. But a red dwarf's zone is so close that planets there are tidally locked, keeping one face to the star.
agingStar.explanation4: As a star swells into a giant it loses mass and its planets' orbits widen. This model ignores the tidal drag that pulls planets in, so it is generous: here Earth survives the Sun's giant phases.
